Paper:
title: Pairing AIS with RF: Analysis of a Markovian Approach for Maritime Data Fusion
summary: Monitoring maritime activities is important for safety and security, particularly for detecting illegal activities, but remains challenging due to the size and complexity of the maritime domain. The Automatic Identification System (AIS) is commonly used for this purpose, despite its known vulnerabilities. In contrast, space-based radio frequency (RF) observations provide an independent source of vessel activity but lack ship identification and therefore cannot identify vessels on their own. Following the CRISP-DM process, this study applies a Pair Hidden Markov Model (PHMM) to align individual RF detections with AIS trajectories, using temporal and spatial information while modeling noise and timing discrepancies. We evaluate it on NOAA AIS data with synthetic RF detections against nearest-neighbor baselines and analyze its errors with bias tests on trajectory length, sampling density, stationarity and AIS--RF distance. The length-corrected Forward score reaches a top-1 precision of $0.7776$ on the validation split of multi-candidate detections, where errors are possible, and an AUC of $0.637$ for detecting dark vessels among the detections that pass the prefilter. With a single RF detection, the score mostly reflects the AIS trajectory itself, and its errors favor longer and more stationary trajectories. A log-odds score, which compares the full model with a null model without match transitions, raises precision to $0.8580$ and AUC to $0.852$. Its length-corrected variant no longer shows a significant bias towards stationary trajectories and short inter-message distances, but still favors candidates farther from the RF detection. A time-weighted nearest-neighbor baseline without fitting remains ahead (precision $0.9013$, AUC $0.904$), so this single-detection, hand-designed PHMM formulation approaches but does not beat it.

Paper:
title: VellSSLH: Sound Type-Guided Selective Speculative Load Hardening for LLVM IR
summary: Constant-time cryptographic programs written in C can still leak secrets during speculative execution. Mispredicted branches may allow instructions to access secret data and expose it through observable behavior. Speculative load hardening (SLH) addresses these leaks, but protecting values unnecessarily can introduce significant runtime overhead. We present VellSSLH, which selectively inserts speculative load hardening at LLVM IR. Programmers specify Public and Secret inputs in annotated C programs, and our analysis infers which values may become secret during speculation. The transformation then inserts misspeculation-flag operations and protections only where needed. VellSCT, our extracted checker, validates the resulting LLVM IR.
  We formalize speculative constant-time (SCT) security by extending Vellvm's LLVM semantics with speculative execution, attacker directives, and leakage observations. Our security type system reasons about SSA joins, symbolic values, poison, pointer provenance, and observable faults, and supports declared declassifications and trusted external services. In Rocq, we prove that programs accepted by the checker satisfy SCT, and that a reference hardening transformation preserves architectural behavior. Evaluated optimized variants are rechecked for SCT but are not covered by this preservation proof. Our mechanized guarantees apply at LLVM IR; security of the generated binary additionally depends on backend and hardware assumptions.
  We evaluate VellSSLH on 24 cryptographic entries on a bare-metal Intel processor. VellSSLH achieves 4.03% lower geometric-mean runtime than LLVM SLH, with 13 comparisons favoring VellSSLH, eight favoring LLVM SLH, and three inconclusive. For X25519, VellSSLH improves runtime by 22.69% over LLVM SLH with only 1.86% overhead over unprotected code. Compared with Ultimate SLH, VellSSLH achieves 19.65% lower runtime.

Paper:
title: Callo: Serving Cache-Miss Requests with Speculative Decoding on Invalidated KV under Prefill-Decode Disaggregation
summary: Agent sessions may involve frequent context edits, which effectively invalidate cached KV state and force requests to wait for re-prefill before decoding. We present Callo, a disaggregated serving system that leverages invalidated KV for speculative drafts to reduce this latency, while verifying drafts against the exact KV after prefill before committing tokens. Callo makes effective use of decode resources by scheduling speculations during periods of underutilization and preempting speculations when drafts are likely to not be accepted. We evaluated Callo on a two-GPU testbed using SWE-agent sessions across three model families, observing all-request speedups of 1.05-1.19x over vLLM at moderate load. We demonstrate that these gains are also realized at scale through cluster-level simulations driven by real-world traces.

Paper:
title: Deterministic ECDSA on secp256k1: the RFC 6979 assumption, a counterexample, and the state of deployed implementations
summary: RFC 6979 derives the ECDSA nonce as $k = F_x(h)$, with $F_x$ HMAC_DRBG keyed by the signing key x. We isolate the assumption its security rests on, A*: at known public key $Q = xG$, the signing transcript under nonces $F_x()$ is indistinguishable from the transcript under uniform nonces. A* suffices, and it is neither PRF security of HMAC nor auxiliary-input PRF security (AI-PRF) of $F_x$. A function $F'(x, h) = P_{Ext(xG)}(h)$ is a PRF under standard assumptions yet leaks x from one signature; the same holds for unmodified RFC 6979 over a compression function that keeps the PRF and dual-PRF properties used in proofs of HMAC, given a collision-resistance premise. A* and AI-PRF are separated in both directions. A* does not imply AI-PRF if the one-bit hidden number problem is hard. Conversely, in the standard model: any AI-PRF can be modified so that it stays one while two chosen-digest signing queries reveal x; under DDH with one public random point, or decisional square Diffie-Hellman without it, there is an AI-PRF whose key is recovered from signatures on two ordinary hashed messages; and a third function, under PRF security and DLP, violates A* while the scheme stays unforgeable. With an ideal compression function, A* follows tightly from DLP in the presence of a randomized-ECDSA signing oracle, and a nonce key independent of x removes the assumption. The secret HMAC message block is $2^{-127.65}$ from uniform on secp256k1, $2^{-32}$ on P-256 and 0.336 on brainpoolP256r1. An audit of 31 secp256k1 implementations finds that 28 sign deterministically without added entropy and that the raw-message deviation from bits2octets of libsecp256k1 before 0.2.0 survives in NBitcoin, dcrd and btcec v2. Low-R grinding needs no assumption beyond A*, and every nonzero Fourier coefficient of the low-R nonce set is below $2^{-116.9}$ unconditionally. We give test vectors for the untested $h >= n$ branch

Paper:
title: CANTraj: Recovering Vehicle Trajectories from CAN Signals in Naturalistic Driving
summary: Open driving releases and usage-based insurance programs often claim to prevent privacy breaches by omitting GPS records when sharing or collecting vehicle data. However, removing GPS coordinates from driving logs does not erase the location information carried by vehicle signals. While prior route-inference attacks have demonstrated that speed, steering, and driving events can be matched to road networks to reconstruct trajectories, existing studies rely on inconsistent prior assumptions and evaluation metrics and are tested only on small, restricted datasets, making their results difficult to compare and their real-world effectiveness uncertain. We release CANTraj, a naturalistic driving dataset pairing decoded CAN events with time-aligned GNSS trajectories (3,940 drives, 454 drivers), and CANTraj-Bench for evaluating trajectory recovery (3,675 drives, 431 drivers, 1,380 hours, 85,919 km). On 776 evaluation drives from 94 unseen drivers, we compare six re-implemented attacks and benchmark baselines under explicit information-access protocols, paired comparisons, and metrics incorporating failures. Experiments show that combining steering signals with road-network constraints yields the largest gain: With a known start and heading, adding steering to speed raises the online map filter's five-minute route recovery from 56% to 87%, with a median average displacement error of 43 m versus 921 m for map-free dead reckoning. Offline beam search recovers 88% of test routes with the heading and 81% without it. Because methods fail on different windows, we also evaluate an LLM harness that selects among candidate routes on 659 five-minute windows; its best configuration recovers 79% of routes on test and 83% on few-shot, outperforming the best baseline on test and matching it on few-shot. Data and code at huggingface.co/datasets/HenryYHW/CANTraj and github.com/WangYuHang-cmd/GPS--CAN.

Paper:
title: They Will See Johnny's Message: A Measurement Study of Post-Quantum Cryptography Across Email Delivery Paths
summary: Harvest-now, decrypt-later (HNDL) attacks make the transition to post-quantum cryptography (PQC) urgent for email. This paper presents a systematic measurement that jointly examines PQC deployment across email service stages, negotiation by communicating peers, and usable message encryption. Endpoint-level support alone does not establish PQC readiness across email workflows because submission, relay, and access use independently negotiated Transport Layer Security (TLS) connections. We therefore combine three snapshots of relay, submission, access, and webmail services associated with the Tranco Top~1M domains with controlled tests of mail clients, sending servers, and OpenPGP and S/MIME implementations. Our measurements reveal a transition concentrated among a few providers, with available capability not consistently translating into actual use. Fewer than half of the domains in each service panel support PQC, and Google alone accounts for approximately 87\% of hybrid-capable relay domains. Only two of eight tested sending providers negotiate PQC with our receiver, although five accept it inbound. When TLS groups are restricted to PQC, four of the six incompatible senders fall back to plaintext where unencrypted SMTP remains permitted. At the message layer, limited native key generation, key-format incompatibilities, and backend integration failures further constrain usable PQC encryption.

Paper:
title: Adaptable Watermarking: Transforming Image Watermarking Models via Lightweight Adapters
summary: We explore the adaptability of neural image watermarking models; the extent to which one watermarking method can be transformed into another through lightweight adaptation. We introduce a framework that enables encoder-decoder watermarking architectures to become modular and upgradable, supporting multiple watermarking styles without re-training full models. Adaptation is performed by attaching a compact parameter-efficient adapter and fine-tuning under a multi-domain residual alignment loss (spatial, gradient, and frequency) while preserving bit accuracy via a secret-loss term. We evaluate this approach across a suite of recent watermarking models, including TrustMark, InvisMark, RoSteALS, HiDDeN, and WAM, demonstrating that adapted encoders closely reproduce target residuals and that adapted decoders recover messages with near-optimal accuracy under standard augmentations and distortions. We show that cross-model adaptation, with applications in interoperable and upgradable watermarking, can be achieved with as few as 1-2M trainable parameters per component (e.g., the 2M decoder adapter used in our multi-decoder inference pipeline).

Paper:
title: Quadratic APN Functions of $\mathbb{F}_2^{10}$ with a Self-Equivalence of Prime Order
summary: Almost perfect nonlinear (APN) functions of $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ have the lowest possible differential uniformity. The only known APN permutation in even dimension, in dimension six, is equivalent to a quadratic APN function with a nontrivial linear self-equivalence; no APN permutation is known for even $n \geq 8$. In a published collection of about 3.8 million quadratic APN classes of dimension eight, at most 0.34% have a nontrivial linear self-equivalence. In dimension ten, the 25 literature classes considered here all have one. We study all quadratic APN functions of $\mathbb{F}_2^{10}$ with such a self-equivalence, which usually confines them to a much smaller linear space. Up to conjugacy and power similarity, self-equivalences of prime order have 299 types. We settle 298 of them. Elementary lemmas exclude 280 types, and exhaustive searches confirm this for 242 of them. The other 18 types are settled by exhaustive searches with exact equivalence certificates. Up to extended affine equivalence, the 298 types contain 29 classes of quadratic APN functions, four of them new. This also classifies the quadratic APN functions with coefficients in a subfield. Exactly 24 classes contain one with coefficients in $\mathbb{F}_4$, and all 3 that contain one with coefficients in $\mathbb{F}_{32}$ are among them. The open type consists of the quadratic canonical triplicate functions. They correspond to maximum additive Hermitian rank-distance codes. Three different searches find only the invariants of 16 classes, all among the 29. We conjecture there are no others. No quadratic APN function in the 298 settled types is Carlet-Charpin-Zinoviev equivalent to a permutation.

Paper:
title: Information-Theoretic Threshold Designated-Verifier Digital Signatures for Resource-Constrained Devices
summary: Digital signatures are synonymous with data integrity and authenticity. Among applications such as e-commerce, software distribution, and instruction processing they play a vital role in the secure communication of data. Within this context and in preparation for quantum adversarial tactics we present three new information-theoretic threshold designated verifier digital signature schemes and prove them secure against \textit{any} adversary under the standard security criterion. title: From Bytes to Behavior: Request-Level Attribution from Live GPU Hidden States
summary: Existing memory forensics for machine learning systems typically targets static artifacts, such as model weights or prompt logs, rather than the transient computational states of a live inference process. title: Forget the Lineage: Forward-Secure, Lineage-Complete Cryptographic Erasure for LLM-Agent Memory

title: The Exact Stabilization Time of Self-Stabilizing Coloring: Mean, Variance, and Distribution
summary: The worst-case stabilization time of a self-stabilizing algorithm usually says little about its typical behavior beyond the order of magnitude. title: Condensing Law of Security Information

title: Securing Multi-Agent Systems by Design
summary: Multi-agent systems solve complex tasks by decomposing them into subtasks, delegating the subtasks to agents, and aggregating the agents' responses using an aggregation rule. Paper:
title: CoordX Types: A Trustless, Swappable Type System for Shared Records
summary: The CoordX Protocol carries signed and encrypted entries between parties. It proves who wrote each entry and who had permission to write it. It does not say what an entry means. That task belongs above the protocol layer. This paper describes the CoordX type system, the layer that gives entries a meaning. A type is a short document that says how to read one part of a shared record: which entries count, what each position means, what a party may do there, and what a party must do next. The type system has two key properties. It is trustless: a type is an ordinary signed object fixed by its digest, and every party evaluates it for itself over entries that the CoordX Protocol has already verified. No party has to trust a server, a registry or another party's software. It is swappable: a type names the interpreter it is written for, so many interpreters, of different capabilities and designs, can be used side by side in one record. We describe how to write type schemas, and we define the expressive power of the schema language. Payloads form a regular language. Entry structure forms a regular tree language. Every rule and every computed value is a total function in the primitive recursive class, so evaluation always halts. We compare this with KQML, FIPA-ACL and CBCL, and we relate it to language-theoretic security.

title: Inferring Sensitive Events in Multi-Mode Cyber-Physical Systems via Scheduling Side Channels
summary: Many cyber-physical systems (CPS) are multi-mode: they switch between operating modes with different tasksets and timing parameters in response to physical events or user activity. We present STAMP, a lightweight attack that needs no knowledge of task parameters or scheduling policy, and works whether or not the system exposes its modes. On a ZoneMinder home-security deployment, STAMP identifies the modes with 94.7% accuracy on unseen hardware, using under 0.5% of one core. On ROS 2 AMCL with the Oxford RobotCar dataset, it identifies which of seven route segments a vehicle traversed with 86.0% accuracy on unseen platforms. A schedule-randomization defense lowers detection recall to 0.53, at which setting only 53.9% as many jobs finish on time. At higher noise ($ε=10$), on-time job completion reduces to 14.4%, while introducing new leakage in 14.1% of the tasksets.

title: Superfluid: Local AI Server for Distributed LLM Inference
summary: Running large language models (LLMs) on local devices keeps data private, removes per-token cost, cuts network latency, and keeps working without a connection. Two shifts now strain how such models are served. On one device, several agents share a locally served model with an interactive user. Across devices, a developer or small team often owns several capable machines from different vendors, which sit idle most of the day because every local server serves one runtime on one machine. Machines with different hardware serve copies of the same model, receive work according to their measured speed, and can join or fail under load without losing a request. title: Evaluating the Robustness of PRNU Source-Camera Attribution to the Fingerprint-Copy Attack: An Open Toolkit with Triangle-Test Detection

title: ForeSpark: Joint Draft and Verification Budget Scheduling for Parallel Speculative Decoding
summary: Parallel drafters accelerate LLM decoding by proposing a whole block of draft tokens in a single forward pass, making them attractive for LLM serving. Paper:
title: Tractable Importance Sampling for Monte Carlo Privacy Accounting
summary: Evaluating tight Differential Privacy (DP) parameters for DP matrix factorization with privacy amplification by sampling requires analyzing high-dimensional, correlated Gaussian mixtures. Because integrating these mixture distributions to find the exact privacy failure probability ($δ$) is analytically intractable, these mechanisms are typically analyzed using Monte Carlo accounting. However, standard sampling suffers from prohibitive variance when estimating small $δ$ associated with strict privacy guarantees, which in turn requires a large sample complexity, making Monte Carlo accounting inefficient. We demonstrate that Monte Carlo accounting can be made much more efficient via importance sampling. We give a shifted importance sampling proposal distribution parameterized by a stretch factor $α> 1$. We prove a closed-form bound $B(α) < 1$ on the support of the importance-weighted estimator that holds identically for both directions of the hockey-stick divergence, show that $B$ is log-convex so that the optimal $α$ is a one-dimensional root-finding problem, and show that the resulting estimator seamlessly plugs into the KL-Hoeffding verification protocol used by past work, with a sample complexity reduced by exactly a factor of $1/B(α^*)$.

Paper:
title: Fair and Efficient Distributed EV Charging Coordination Using Threshold Cryptography and Machine Learning
summary: Distributed coordination of electric vehicle (EV) charging with the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) keeps EV constraints private but assumes that every participant follows the algorithm. This assumption fails in practice, where a biased operator or a man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacker can send inconsistent signals to different EVs, and compromised EVs can deviate from their prescribed updates. We first prove that attacks by such arbitrarily malicious, i.e., Byzantine, participants do not prevent convergence and therefore remain undetected, and derive the most damaging attack in closed form. We then propose a framework that combines a threshold-signed broadcast with upload recomputation, which detects every deviation without false alarms at linear instead of quadratic communication cost. To keep the optimization running, each affected EV recovers locally with a certified, fleet-aware machine learning price forecast, and we prove that the optimization remains convergent with a recovery cost bounded by the shape of the forecast error. Simulation results with real-world load, price, and charging data show that a biased operator raises the annual cost of disadvantaged EVs by 132.7% and lowers that of advantaged EVs by 49.3% without changing the aggregate load, whereas the defense limits all cost changes to 2.6%. An external MITM attacker raises the cost of its victims by 57.6%, the peak load by 5.8%, and the grid cost by 15.8%, whereas the defense keeps them within 1.1%, 0.2%, and 0.3% of benign operation. With up to 70% of the EVs attacked, the recovery converges in at least 97.8% of the runs.

title: Performance-Portable Exact Gaussian Process Regression in Python via SYCL and oneMath
summary: Modern multi-vendor GPU environments force a choice between portable code and native performance. GPRat is an open-source Python library for exact Gaussian process regression built on the HPX asynchronous many-task runtime, tiled algorithms, and CPU/CUDA BLAS backends. We contribute a UXL Foundation oneMath backend with a hybrid HPX/SYCL design, extending GPRat to AMD and Intel GPUs. Paper:
title: Adversarial Attacks on Downstream Weather Forecasting Models: Application to Tropical Cyclone Trajectory Prediction
summary: Deep learning-based weather forecasting (DLWF) models leverage past weather observations to generate future forecasts, supporting a wide range of downstream applications, including tropical cyclone (TC) prediction. In this paper, we investigate the vulnerability of these models to adversarial attacks, where subtle perturbations to upstream forecasts can alter downstream TC trajectory predictions. Crafting perturbed inputs to steer downstream outputs toward attacker-specified trajectories is a challenging problem for several reasons. First, conventional TC detection systems are opaque, non-differentiable black boxes, making standard gradient-based attacks infeasible. Second, the extreme rarity of TC events leads to a severe class imbalance problem, making it difficult to develop attack methods that produce realistic-looking cyclone paths aligned with target trajectories. To overcome these limitations, we propose Cyc-Attack, a novel method for perturbing the forecasts of DLWF models to generate adversarial trajectories. The proposed method uses a differentiable surrogate model to approximate the TC detector's output, enabling the application of gradient-based attacks. Cyc-Attack also employs a skewness-aware loss function with a kernel dilation strategy to address the severe class imbalance problem. Distance-based gradient weighting and regularization strategies are also introduced to constrain perturbations to eliminate unrealistic-looking TC paths. Our experiments show that Cyc-Attack achieves a higher true positive rate in matching the target trajectories, along with lower false alarm rates and stealthier perturbations than conventional attack methods. We further demonstrate that the adversarial upstream forecasts generated by Cyc-Attack can be leveraged as initial guidance to train an end-to-end model for learning adversarial input samples that would induce target trajectories.

Paper:
title: Online Allocation with Differential Privacy
summary: We study private online allocation problems, where allocation decisions must satisfy differential privacy (DP) to protect sensitive user information while optimizing performance under limited resources. We first formalize differential privacy notions suited to different privacy requirements in online allocation and establish the fundamental performance limits of any algorithm under these definitions. Based on these insights, we propose PPOA, a privacy-preserving meta algorithm for online allocation, and establish sufficient conditions under which PPOA preserves Joint DP (JDP) or Local DP (LDP) while achieving asymptotically near-optimal performance. Building on these conditions, PPOA can be instantiated into a variety of concrete algorithms. In particular, we present the specific designs, which include PPOA-DMD that preserves JDP and LDP and PPOA-FTRL that preserves JDP. We analyze their performance under both adversarial and stochastic settings and characterize the fundamental trade-offs between DP and allocation performance. Finally, we demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed algorithms via numerical experiments on AI model routing in battery-powered edge systems.

Paper:
title: I2C-GRPO: Insight Importance Checklist for Reinforcement Learning in a Multi-Agent DDoS Alert Triage Workflow
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used for investigative tasks over incomplete evidence, such as cybersecurity alert triage, but reinforcement learning (RL) for such tasks is difficult: intermediate steps have no verifiable labels, rollouts are costly, and outcome rewards are sparse. We propose Insight Importance Checklist (I2C)-GRPO, a checklist reward for intermediate investigation steps. For each decision point, a panel of expert LLMs proposes investigative actions, their atomic forensic insights are extracted, and a separate three-model ranker panel orders the insights by importance. A reward model checks which ranked insights a candidate action targets and returns their consensus-weighted coverage. Because actions are scored without being executed, the reward is a proxy for expected investigative value, and training reduces to a one-step contextual bandit over fixed investigation prefixes. From a soft-computing perspective, the reward is an additive fuzzy measure whose rank-exponent weights act as an ordered weighted averaging (OWA)-type operator; one exponent sets its orness, i.e., how strongly the reward concentrates on the top of the judges' consensus.
  We train an open-weight Qwen3-4B Triage Agent within a fixed multi-agent Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) alert-triage workflow on DARPA 2000 LLDOS 1.0 and test it on an independent CSE-CIC-IDS2018 DDoS trace. Across three training seeds, the agent reaches a mean F1-score of 0.869, 5.9 and 9.7 points above uniform insight weights and DIVA, and a false-positive rate of 4.9% versus 16.4% for GPT-5-mini. Within the weighting family, false positives fall only at the highest-orness weighting evaluated. All claims are limited to DDoS alert triage; the code, task contexts, and ranked insight dataset will be released.

title: A Push Down the Mountain: Framing Effects and Internal State Interventions on Collusive Behavior in a Long-Horizon LLM Agent
summary: Can sustained gain-loss (valence) framing sway an LLM agent toward market manipulation? We place Gemma 3 12B into the seat of a defendant in the London silver-fixing litigation, in a market simulation built from real case transcripts. Across 260 simulations, the agent is asked to collude on the price of silver by a counterparty. We draw from behavioral economics to vary the counterparty's requests across four categorical frames: gain, loss, blame and credit. We also add pressure from the agent's management, as well as endorsement by another defendant. In Phase II, we extract the internal states induced by texts evoking each frame and rerun our experiment with those states injected at the model's layer 22.
  In Phase I, loss framing raised participation to 25% (p = 0.007), and blame to 33% (p = 0.0003), compared to only 5% under neutral framing. A second bank's endorsement raised participation under credit (praise) from 18% to 40% (Holm p = 0.027). Pressure from management raised trading volume 10-19 times but did not raise collusion. In Phase II, injected states pointed the other way. Loss and blame states made the agent more vigilant, refusing all 60 requests (p < 0.001). Gain and credit states raised collusion to 32% from 13% with no state (p = 0.051). At one saved decision, when UBS asked directly to sell through an identified stop-loss, injected states led the agent to sell in 37 of 40 replies, versus 1 of 10 with no state and 0 of 10 with a random state of the same strength.
